newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND, RUSSIA TO CONSULT OFTEN ON SECURITY-RYBKIN.
newsitem.headline: POLAND, RUSSIA TO CONSULT OFTEN ON SECURITY-RYBKIN.

text.p: The secretary of Russia's Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, ended a visit to Warsaw on Tuesday with an agreement to start frequent consultations and said he was glad Moscow could no longer dictate to Poland.
During two days of talks Rybkin upheld Moscow's arguments against the expansion of NATO, which former Soviet satellites Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary hope to join by 1999.
But Rybkin, who chose Poland for his first foreign visit as head of the policy-making council, told a news conference:
"As for the entry of specific countries to NATO, thank God we have lived until times when we cannot impose anything or prescribe anything. We see this as our greatest achievement."

Rybkin repeatedly affirmed that he expected Russia would clinch a treaty with NATO on May 27, as predicted by President Boris Yeltsin last week, which would resolve most of Moscow's fears over the alliance's eastward expansion.
"The compromise, which I deeply hope will be signed on May 27, eliminates a whole range -- the majority -- of fears Russia has had so far," Rybkin said.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said in Prague on Monday this date was possible but Russia would continue to oppose the expansion of NATO. The organisation plans at its Madrid summit in July to invite new members to begin entry talks.
Russia insists that new NATO members should not be allowed to improve their existing military infrastructure to bring it up to the pact's standards, a demand that NATO has refused.

At the conference held with Marek Siwiec, head of Poland's presidential National Security Office, Rybkin said they had agreed to create a mechanism for cooperation including frequent working meetings to settle worries.

Poland's relations with Moscow, whose dominance it escaped after the 1989 fall of communism, have since been fraught with coldness and incidents such as this year's long detention in Russia's Far East of a Polish fishing trawler.
Siwiec said bilateral ties were at last improving.
"There was a time when we spoke with Russia on our knees, and a time when we tried to speak with Russia holding our noses haughtily in the air," Siwiec said.
"Now the time has come when we can talk with Russia looking deep into each other's eyes, staying with our standpoint but finding understanding if not necessarily agreement," he said.

Rybkin said he had agreed with Poland's interior minister on stepped up cooperation against crime, drugs and bribery and had discussed contacts with the defence minister, including a meeting soon between the two armed forces chiefs of staff.
He said he had told Polish parliamentarians Russia wanted to learn about how to adjust laws to take account of reforms -- in many of which Poland was more advanced than Russia.

Asked whether Poland might consider Russian fighter aircraft when it decides on a major contract being contested among U.S. and European firms to update its air force, Siwiec said Warsaw was open to some defence purchases from Russia.
But he added: "I don't want to give the impression that we can be an army of NATO and equip ourselves outside of NATO. This would be a wrong impression."
Rybkin, who met Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski on Tuesday, stressed the need to further boost bilateral trade with totalled $4.2 billion in 1996. REUTER
